value.overview: The Greater Ani (Crotophaga major) is a large, glossy black member of the cuckoo family. It is strongly associated with water and usually lives in small, noisy social groups. Unlike the more familiar Smooth-billed and Groove-billed Anis, it favors wooded riverbanks, lake margins, flooded forest, mangroves, and other forested habitats close to wetlands. Its long rounded tail, broad bill, pale eye, and blue-green sheen make it distinctive where it occurs.
value.classification: The Greater Ani belongs to the cuckoo family, Cuculidae, in the order Cuculiformes. It is one of four highly social ani species in the subfamily Crotophaginae.
value.identification: This is the largest ani, measuring roughly 45–50 cm including its long tail. Adults are entirely dark, with glossy black plumage that may show blue, green, or purple reflections on the wings and tail. The bill is large, deep, and laterally broad, while the iris is pale yellow to whitish. The long tail is rounded rather than sharply pointed. Greater Anis are commonly encountered in groups and often remain near water or forest edges.
value.rangeHabitat: The Greater Ani ranges from eastern Panama and Trinidad through much of tropical South America to northern Argentina. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly as a localized and uncommon species in suitable lowland habitat, especially toward the southwestern Pacific region near rivers, lakes, wetlands, and forest margins; it is not widespread throughout the country. Preferred sites include mangrove edges, flooded woodland, gallery forest, riverbanks, and semi-open forest bordering slow-moving water. It generally avoids dry, open agricultural landscapes favored by some other anis.
value.migrationStatus: The species is generally resident or locally mobile, although seasonal movements are reported in parts of its broad range. In Costa Rica, it is best treated as an uncommon local resident or irregularly recorded species rather than a regular long-distance migrant; reliable evidence for a consistent Costa Rican migration pattern is limited.
value.breeding: Greater Anis breed cooperatively in groups, commonly involving several pairs and sometimes additional helpers. The group builds a large, deep cup-shaped nest from sticks and leaves, usually in a tree near or overhanging water, or in vegetation beside wetlands. Several females may lay in the same communal nest. Group members share nest construction, incubation, defense, and feeding of the young. Nesting success depends strongly on maintaining trees, shrubs, and emergent vegetation along quiet waterways.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of large insects, including beetles, grasshoppers, caterpillars, dragonflies, and other arthropods. Greater Anis also take spiders and may eat small lizards, frogs, other small vertebrates, fruits, berries, and seeds. They usually forage in loose groups along forest edges and watercourses, searching foliage, branches, bark, and the ground. Their social foraging and conspicuous movements can make a group easier to detect than a single bird.
value.behavior: Greater Anis are highly social and typically travel in groups that may include several adults and young birds. They produce deep, resonant, sometimes mechanical-sounding calls and often vocalize together. Groups move through low and middle vegetation, especially beside rivers and lakes, and may rest communally. Cooperative breeding, joint territory defense, and shared care of nestlings are prominent features of their behavior. Birds can be secretive in dense riverside vegetation despite their loud calls and dark plumage.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not known with confidence. Available assessments do not indicate a decline severe enough to qualify the species for a threatened category. In Costa Rica, its limited and localized occurrence may partly reflect specialized habitat requirements and incomplete documentation.
